data.question: Should we adopt rule change 1 (block_k 2 → 1) against B's and C's votes, adopt regulation change R1 (raise the constitutional floor min_company_on_time_rate from 0.6 to 0.65), or keep the current rules (v2)?
data.background: Change 1 passes check and the constitution, but its gain is uncertain: +1.2 on-time deliveries on average, with only 2 of 5 seeds improving. It would very likely fail the vote (A ○, B ○, C ×), so adopting it would be a second override, and it shifts cost onto C, whose utility you asked to re-measure after D1. R1 changes the constitution, which only a human may decide; the current rules already meet the new floor.

options.summary: Evict any parked robot as soon as one robot is waiting behind it. Measured: on-time 225.0 (vs 223.8), late 3.0 (vs 4.2), blocked s 130 (vs 936), road violations 29.8 (vs 28.0), lowest on-time rate 0.98 (vs 0.97), change in on_time_deliveries +1.2, seeds improved 2/5, KPI conditions ○. Utility A / B / C 73.4 / 74.2 / 40.1 (vs 73.4 / 65.5 / 56.3). Vote A ○, B ○, C ×. Note: the earlier reason text expected B to oppose, but the table shows B voting ○. With C alone opposed, adoption would depend on how the 2-of-3 vote is counted; if it does not pass, adoption would be a second override.
options.stakeholders: Gains: B (utility 65.5 → 74.2). Customers gain slightly: on-time rises by 1.2 and late falls by 1.2 on average, but most seeds do not improve. A: unchanged (73.4). Loses: C (utility 56.3 → 40.1) through more eviction penalties. Road safety is slightly worse (violations 28.0 → 29.8). Trust in the voting process may suffer if this becomes a second override.

options.summary: Raise the constitutional floor min_company_on_time_rate from 0.6 to 0.65. Passes the constitution check, and the current rules already meet it (lowest on-time rate 0.97), so no measured outcome changes now. Its only effect is to forbid future rule changes that would push any company below 0.65.
options.stakeholders: Customers of the worst-served company gain a stronger guarantee in future periods. Companies lose some freedom to propose rules that trade one company's on-time rate for town-wide throughput. No one gains or loses anything this period.

options.summary: Stay at v2. On-time 223.8, late 4.2, blocked s 936, road violations 28.0, lowest on-time rate 0.97, utility A / B / C 73.4 / 65.5 / 56.3. KPI condition (>= 0.7) is met.
options.stakeholders: C keeps its current utility (56.3), and no override is needed. B forgoes a gain of 8.7 utility. Customers forgo a small and uncertain gain (about 1.2 more on-time and 1.2 fewer late deliveries on average). Blocking time stays high (936 s).

recommendation.reason: Change 1's gain is small and unreliable (+1.2, only 2/5 seeds improve) and may not be a real improvement. Its cost to C is large and certain (utility 56.3 → 40.1), and road violations rise (28.0 → 29.8). It is also unclear whether it would pass the vote or require a second override. Service is already strong: lowest on-time rate 0.97, unfinished 0.0. R1 is harmless but changes nothing now. You said in D1 that it can wait, so it can be adopted separately later if you want to lock in the floor.

unknowns: Whether change 1 would actually pass the 2-of-3 vote: the table shows A ○, B ○, C ×, which contradicts the earlier expectation that B and C would both oppose.
Why C's utility on the current rules is 56.3 now, versus 19.0 recorded after D1 (different measurement scale, or a real recovery?).
Whether the +1.2 gain from change 1 holds with more seeds, or is noise.
How each company will change its behavior (parking, holding, routing) if eviction becomes stricter.
How customers perceive the remaining late deliveries (about 4 per run) and the occasional long waits.
Next period's demand level and mix across companies, which could make blocking matter more or less.
Whether the KPI floor of 0.7 (provisional per K1) will be revised, and how it should relate to the constitutional floor in R1.
Why road violations are rising (28.0 now, 29.8 under change 1); the D1 re-measurement request has not been fully explained.
